Look, I have to run in two minutes, so I’ll just point you where to look. For the specific brand of food, when did you adopt her? The shelter should have left the bag they were feeding or a transition guide on the label. Use that for three weeks to avoid a stomach ache, then check the veterinary clinic’s lobby brochures for the local vet’s approved starter list. They have laminated sheets with exact caloric needs for three-month-old Labs right next to the checkout counter.

As for how often, it’s usually three times a day at that size. You can set alarms on your phone for morning, afternoon, and evening to keep it regular. Don’t snack in between. The puppy’s routine sets yours, so just stick to the clock. If you miss a window, skip it and wait for the next scheduled time so you don’t confuse her stomach.

Treats are tricky because you don’t want to spoil her appetite or ruin her teeth. High-value training rewards like small pieces of boiled chicken or commercial soft-training bites are fine, but keep them under five percent of her daily calories. A good rule is one small treat per successful command. Again, the vet techs can weigh out a sample portion if you’re unsure.

Honestly, the breeder or rescueordinator who gave you the paperwork has a contact number. Call them directly. They know her history, her likes and dislikes, and exactly what she ate yesterday. That’s the fastest way to get accurate, personalized answers without guessing. I really need to go now.

I actually have to head out in about thirty seconds, so I can’t go into recipes or socialization timelines. Your best bet is to ask the puppy trainer who’s leading the newborn-class workshop at the local pet supply store—they’ll have batched recipes and low-risk puppy meet-up schedules. If you just want to avoid making bad choices, search for “puppy-safe baked treats” on reputable canine nutrition blogs and pick one that uses single-protein ingredients and no added salt or sweetener.

Also, a lot of first-time owners join a puppy socialization circle; you’ll get meet-and-greet access and the trainer will model the correct approach distance and duration. It saves you trial and error. Catch you on the flip side.

Switching food is a big deal, and honestly, I shouldn't be giving you medical advice while I'm trying to catch my train. You need to talk to your vet about her specific growth curve. Labs grow fast and then stop abruptly, so timing is everything. If you switch too early, you risk nutritional gaps; too late, and you risk obesity. The clinic staff can look at her rib check and tell you exactly when she’s done growing.

For the transition, it’s just a slow mix over ten days. Start with ninety percent old food, ten percent new. Bump the new ratio by ten percent every day until you’re at one hundred. It sounds tedious, but skipping this guarantees three days of upset tums and cleanup. Trust the process, follow the bag instructions, and call your vet if she skips two meals.
